newsitem.title: FRANCE: Ex-world partners recall Mitterrand's role.
newsitem.headline: Ex-world partners recall Mitterrand's role.

text.p: Former international partners of the late French president Francois Mitterrand praised on Thursday his work for peace and development at a UNESCO seminar marking the first anniversary of his death.
Ex-leaders of Third World nations hailed his struggle throughout his 14-year rule for a fairer sharing of world resources and to lighten the foreign debt burden of the poorest countries.

"During these years of upheaval...his voice was heard in all forums, during all crises to protect the dignity, security and freedom of every man and woman and guarantee their access to health, education and welfare," said UNESCO Director-General Federico Mayor.
But attendance at the two-day meeting, dubbed "Great Witnesses", fell short of the organisers' expectations.
Former U.S. and Soviet leaders George Bush and Mikhail Gorbachev declined the invitation because of previous commitments. Egyptian President Hosni Mubarak stayed away but sent a message.
Palestinian leader Yasser Arafat, Israeli ex-premier Shimon Peres and the former United Nations chief Boutros Boutros-Ghali were due to address Friday's closing session.

But Cuban President Fidel Castro, who toured France in 1994 in a rare visit to the West, let a question mark hang over another visit. Organisers said he had not confirmed attendance, and a spokeswoman for the Cuban embassy said she was still waiting for a hint from Havana on whether he would come or not.
Roland Dumas, Mitterrand's long-serving foreign minister, emotionally quoted some of the Socialist leader's ringing statements on the need to close the wealth gap.
"Failing to cut the widening gap between rich and poor countries will condemn the world to pitiless conflicts," he quoted Mitterrand as saying.

He recalled major initiatives for development at the 1981 Cancun summit, for democracy at the 1990 Franco-African summit in La Baule, and Mitterrand's 1989 decision to cancel the public debt of the world's 35, mostly African, poorest states.

Francoise de Panafieu, France's envoy to the U.N. Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organisation, speaking on behalf of President Jacques Chirac, said Mitterrand had followed in the path laid out by post-war leader General Charles de Gaulle which would be continued by Chirac.
"France, home of human rights, will work for the development of everyone as Mitterrand and de Gaulle did. This is the hyphen between our presidents," she said.

Former Senegalese prime minister Habib Thiam took a thinly-veiled swipe at Chirac's tough immigration policies, recalling that Mitterrand had upheld a French tradition by granting residence rights to many illegal African immigrants.

Chirac's conservative government has been embarrassed by protests from African immigrants who claim that a 1993 tightening of immigration regulations has deprived them of residence rights they once enjoyed.

Ex-European Commission president Jacques Delors and other former major European players were later in the day to discuss Mitterrand's role as one of the main champions of European unity to prevent war from returning to the continent.
